title: Segment Tree: Range Sum Query, Mutable
oneLiner: Design a NumArray that supports update(index, val) and sumRange(left, right) on a changing array, both in O(log n).
keyTakeaway: Prefix sums make queries O(1) but every update O(n); a segment tree makes both O(log n). Each node stores the sum of a range, an update rewrites one leaf and its log n ancestors, and a query adds up the few nodes that sit completely inside [left, right]. Store it in an array of size 4n with node k's children at 2k and 2k + 1 (or 2k + 1 and 2k + 2 when the root is 0).
explanation:
Build a class NumArray over an int array with two operations: update(index, val) sets nums[index] = val, and sumRange(left, right) returns nums[left] + ... + nums[right], inclusive. Updates and queries are mixed in any order, up to tens of thousands of each, so both must be fast. This is LeetCode 307 and a classic follow-up to the Prefix Sums lesson: a prefix array answers sumRange in O(1), but changing one element shifts every prefix after it, an O(n) repair per update.

A segment tree is a binary tree where every node stores the sum of a contiguous range of indices. The root covers [0, n - 1]. A node covering [lo, hi] splits at mid = (lo + hi) / 2: its left child covers [lo, mid] and its right child [mid + 1, hi]. Leaves cover a single index. It is stored in a plain array the same way a heap is: with the root at 1, node k has children 2k and 2k + 1, and an array of 4n slots is always big enough.

Build (O(n)): recurse to the leaves, set each leaf to its element, and on the way back up set each node to left + right.

Update (O(log n)): walk from the root towards the leaf for index, choosing the left child when index <= mid. Set the leaf, then recompute every node on the way back up. That is one node per level, and the tree has about log2(n) levels.

Query (O(log n)): ask the root for [left, right]. A node whose range is completely outside the query returns 0, the identity for sums (the value that changes nothing when added). A node completely inside returns its stored sum without going deeper. A node that partly overlaps asks both children and adds the answers. The query range is split into at most about 2 log n fully covered nodes, so very little is visited.

A Fenwick tree (see the Range Queries tool) also solves this in O(log n) with less code: keep a copy of nums, and turn update into add(index + 1, val - nums[index]). Either is a full-marks answer; say which you chose and why.

The harness builds new NumArray(nums), then runs each operation in order: "update" with [index, val] and "sumRange" with [left, right]. It returns the results of the sumRange calls. Indices are always valid. The visualization builds a tree over 8 numbers, updates one, and runs a query.

recognitionSignals: Range sums (or counts) on an array that also CHANGES between queries.
"Design a class" with update(i, val) and a range query, each to be faster than O(n).
Prefix sums would work if the array were static, but updates would force a rebuild.
gotchas: Size the array 4n, not 2n: with the recursive split, a tree over n elements that is not a power of two can use indices past 2n.
Outside a query a node must return the identity (0 for a sum), not skip silently; and the inside check is left <= lo && hi <= right, both ends inclusive.
An update has to recompute every ancestor on the way back up, not just the leaf.
With a Fenwick tree, update sets a value, so add the difference val - nums[index] and remember the new value.
confusableWith: Prefix Sums: Answer Range-Sum Queries in O(1) (Patterns) is the static version: no updates, O(1) queries.
Segment Tree: Range Minimum Query with Updates (this track) is the same tree with min instead of +, which a Fenwick tree cannot do.

complexity.note: Per operation: update rewrites one leaf and its ancestors, one node per level, and sumRange visits at most about four nodes per level. Building is a one-off O(n). The tree array has 4n slots (a Fenwick tree uses n + 1), which is still O(n).
